# MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation

Kai Chen Affiliation: State Key Laboratory for Novel Software
Technology, Nanjing University    Xinfeng Li Affiliation: Nanyang
Technological University    Tianpei Yang^(\*) Affiliation: State Key
Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University    Hewei
Wang Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University
   Wei Dong Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University    Yang Gao
Affiliation: State Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing
University

###### Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant progress in various
fields. However, challenges remain in Multi-Disciplinary Team (MDT)
medical consultations. Current research enhances reasoning through role
assignment, task decomposition, and accumulation of medical experience.
Multi-role collaboration in MDT consultations often results in
excessively long dialogue histories. This increases the model’s
cognitive burden and degrades both efficiency and accuracy. Some methods
only store treatment histories. They do not extract effective experience
or reflect on errors. This limits knowledge generalization and system
evolution. We propose a multi-agent MDT medical consultation framework
based on LLMs to address these issues. Our framework uses consensus
aggregation and a residual discussion structure for multi-round
consultations. It also employs a Correct Answer Knowledge Base
(CorrectKB) and a Chain-of-Thought Knowledge Base (ChainKB) to
accumulate consultation experience. These mechanisms enable the
framework to evolve and continually improve diagnosis rationality and
accuracy. Experimental results on the MedQA and PubMedQA datasets
demonstrate that our framework achieves accuracies of 90.1% and 83.9%,
respectively, and that the constructed knowledge bases generalize
effectively across test sets from both datasets. Our code is publicly
available at:
[https://kaichennj.github.io/MDTeamGPT](https://kaichennj.github.io/MDTeamGPT-Main).

## 1 Introduction

When diagnosing and treating complex diseases, a single-specialty
medical perspective frequently proves insufficient to address patients’
comprehensive and precise healthcare needs, thereby necessitating the
implementation of a Multi-Disciplinary Team (MDT) and diversified
clinical perspectives [Macken et al. (2022)](#bib.bib20); [Zhou and Xu
(2023)](#bib.bib41). MDT facilitates the development of more accurate
and holistic therapeutic strategies through systematic integration of
expertise across medical disciplines [Makary (2011)](#bib.bib22).
Nevertheless, the organization of interdisciplinary consultations
demands substantial temporal and human resources, while remaining
vulnerable to procedural oversights, cognitive biases, and communication
inefficiencies [Burton et al. (2022)](#bib.bib2). Such systemic
challenges may ultimately compromise healthcare quality and adversely
affect patient outcomes.

![Refer to caption](2503.13856v1/ACL-Fig1.png)

Figure 1: The lead physician consolidates and refines the discussion
outcomes from the current round of agents by categorizing them into four
detailed categories: consistency, conflict, independence, and
integration, thereby enhancing the overall diagnostic clarity.

Large Language Models (LLMs), with their massive parameter sizes and
extensive training on vast knowledge bases from diverse domains,
demonstrate strong reasoning abilities and zero-shot generalization
capabilities [Achiam et al. (2023)](#bib.bib1); [Touvron et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib33). These capabilities have led many researchers to
explore the potential application of LLMs in medical MDT
diagnostics [Kim et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12); [Chen et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib4). Leveraging LLMs as autonomous agents offers a
promising way to improve medical consultations by human doctors.

However, the application of LLMs in MDT diagnostics faces two primary
challenges. First, privacy constraints and the lack of standardized data
storage result in scarce medical consultation data, hindering the
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of large models. Secondly, although LLMs
have been fine-tuned with medical knowledge, they remain prone to
hallucination issues [Ye et al. (2023)](#bib.bib37); [Pal et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib24). In the medical field, such hallucinations can
result in severe medical incidents even with minor errors [Nori et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib23).

Multi-agent based on LLMs enhances medical reasoning by stimulating
latent medical knowledge through multi-round interactions and
significantly reduces the occurrence of hallucinations [Liu et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib17); [Du et al. (2023)](#bib.bib5). Recent research in
this domain has primarily focused on role configuration [Tang et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib32); [Long et al. (2024)](#bib.bib18), subtask
decomposition [Pandey et al. (2024)](#bib.bib25), clinical environment
simulation [Schmidgall et al. (2024)](#bib.bib31), and the accumulation
of medical experience [Wei et al. (2024)](#bib.bib35); [Li et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib14). However, several challenges remain. First,
multi-role interactions often result in excessively long dialogues. As
contextual information accumulates, the cognitive load on the model
increases, negatively impacting response efficiency and
accuracy [Maharana et al. (2024)](#bib.bib21). Second, some studies rely
on simply storing diagnostic histories without effectively integrating
correct diagnostic experiences or reflecting on errors, which may lead
to biases when handling detailed information [Li et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib13). Finally, enhancing the generalization ability of
systems in preserving medical experiences [Qian et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib27) is crucial for achieving self-evolution and
leveraging collective intelligence.

In this work, we propose a self-evolving LLM-based multi-agent framework
(MDTeamGPT) for multi-disciplinary team medical consultation. This
framework incorporates various doctor roles and supporting roles, where
a "patient" role arrives with specific background information and
medical questions. The Primary Care Doctor assigns the patient to the
most suitable specialist agents based on the patient’s condition.
Subsequently, the specialist agents engage in a multi-round of
discussion, sharing relevant information. After each round, a lead
physician summarizes and organizes the discussion outcomes, categorizing
them into Consistency, Conflict, Independence, and Integration, as
illustrated in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation").
In the subsequent discussion rounds, agents refer to the information
stored in the Historical Shared Pool based on the residual discussion
structure. Once a consensus is reached through multiple rounds of
deliberation, the final consultation outcome is reviewed and filtered by
a Safety and Ethics Reviewer before presenting the final results and
recommendations. At this stage, the consultation outcomes are further
categorized based on their correctness and stored in distinct knowledge
bases, serving as references to enhance future consultations. Overall,
the main contributions of our work are threefold:

- •
  We propose an MDT-based multi-agent medical consultation framework
  that incorporates a lead physician mechanism and a residual discussion
  structure to effectively integrate multi-round discussion outcomes.
  This design reduces the cognitive load on agents, thereby enhancing
  the accuracy of reasoning and decision-making.
- •
  The framework employs an adaptive learning mechanism that leverages
  both correct and incorrect diagnostic experiences, progressively
  accumulating and strengthening transferable reasoning capabilities.
- •
  Experimental results demonstrate that the framework, utilizing 600
  rounds of consultation experience, achieves accuracies of 90.1% on the
  MedQA dataset and 83.9% on the PubMedQA dataset. Cross-dataset tests
  further confirm that the knowledge bases retain generalizable
  reasoning skills, not just isolated consultation data.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 LLM-based Multi-Agent Collaboration

Well-structured multi-agent systems can significantly reduce errors and
enhance interaction efficiency [Qian et al. (2024c)](#bib.bib29); [Park
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib26); [Du et al. (2024)](#bib.bib6); [Qian et al.
(2024d)](#bib.bib30). ChatDev [Qian et al. (2024c)](#bib.bib29) splits
tasks into subtasks managed by an instructor and an assistant, using
multi-round inquiries to mitigate hallucinations. MACNET [Qian et al.
(2024d)](#bib.bib30) adopts a directed acyclic graph with topological
sorting for interactive reasoning, and MetaGPT [Hong et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib8) encodes SOPs for roles akin to a software company,
effectively coordinating specialized expertise. However, these methods
primarily focus on software development and face applicability
challenges in medical consultations. Medagents [Tang et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib32) assigns distinct doctor roles to each LLM-Agent and
uses consensus voting, but lacks a robust strategy, risking collective
hallucinations [Chen et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib3). Additionally, these
methods rely on static structures limited by zero-shot capabilities.

### 2.2 Experience Utilization

Inspired by human knowledge acquisition mechanisms, equipping LLM-Agents
with reflective memory can enhance their problem-solving
capabilities [Zhong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib40). ExpeL [Zhao et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib39) accumulates experiences from past successes and
applies this knowledge during reasoning. Co-Learning [Qian et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib27) focuses on collecting experience-driven heuristics
from prior actions, thus enabling agents to handle novel tasks more
flexibly. IER [Qian et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib28) permits LLM-Agents to
iteratively refine accumulated experiences throughout task execution.
Selfevolve [Jiang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib9) employs LLMs both as
knowledge providers and as self-reflective programmers, allowing agents
to evolve through reflective processes. Agent Hospital [Li et al.
(2024c)](#bib.bib15) utilizes medical record libraries and experience
databases to accumulate diagnostic data, enhancing prompts for medical
agents and supporting their evolution. However, the lack of abstraction,
summarization, and reflection on erroneous cases limits the ability to
fully leverage valuable insights from mistakes.

### 2.3 Discussion and Aggregation

An effective discussion process can significantly enhance
LLM-Multi-Agent performance. The Nominal Group Technique (NGT) [Ven and
Delbecq (1974)](#bib.bib34) is a structured decision-making method that
moves teams from individual ideation to collective consensus through
four stages: personal idea generation, round-robin sharing, focused
discussion, and voting. Building on this principle, LLM Discussion [Lu
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib19) augments the creative potential of LLMs by
dividing conversations into initiation, discussion, and convergence
phases, thereby promoting iterative and divergent exchanges among
multiple agents.

## 3 Method

![Refer to caption](2503.13856v1/acl1.png)

Figure 2: Overview of our MDTeamGPT medical consultations framework: (A)
arranging strategically specialist doctors based on the patient’s
specific condition; (B) orchestrating multi-round collaborative
consultations with organized clinical information; (C) summarizing and
outputting the final diagnostic and treatment recommendations.

In this section, we provide a detailed description of our medical
consultation framework. Within this framework, we have established a set
of specialist doctor Agent roles, $`\mathcal{S}`$ (General Internal
Medicine Doctor, General Surgeon, Pediatrician, Obstetrician and
Gynecologist, Radiologist, Neurologist, Pathologist, Pharmacist), and a
set of auxiliary Agent roles, $`\mathcal{A}`$ (Primary Care Doctor, Lead
Physician, Chain-of-Thought Reviewer, Safety and Ethics Reviewer). The
roles within $`\mathcal{A}`$ do not directly participate in the
consultation process; their functions are elaborated in Sections 3.2 and
3.3. This role setup broadens the framework’s applicability to diverse
complex medical cases. The prompt templates for all roles are provided
in Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation").
Figure
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")
presents an overview of the proposed framework, which is divided into
three critical stages.

### 3.1 Aranging Specialist Doctors

When the patient agent comes for a consultation carrying personal
background $`C`$ and medical problem $`Q`$, the Primary Care Doctor
Agent assigns specialist doctor Agents based on the specific
circumstances of the patient. Before making the final decision, the
Primary Care Doctor Agent provides Reasons for the selection. To ensure
the triage doctor’s output is more accurate and structured, we configure
the Primary Care Doctor Agent with a few-shot example as a reference.
The workflow is as follows: This description can be expressed by the
following formula:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\text{Reasons},\text{Roles}=\text{LLM}\left(\text{Agents}\mid C,Q\right).
``` |  | (1) |

|     |                                   |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{Roles}\subseteq\mathcal{S}.
       ```                                |     | (2) |

This approach prevents information contamination caused by an excess of
irrelevant expert agents. During configuration, we provide the Primary
Care Doctor Agent with a limited number of cases, encouraging it to
output responses in a prescribed format. An example is presented below:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 3.2 Multi-Round Consultations

Once the specialist doctors for the consultation have been determined,
the consultation process officially begins. In the initial round, each
specialist doctor presents their opinion based on the patient’s
condition, denoted as $`S_{1,k}`$ (where $`S_{1,k}`$ represents the
response of the $`k`$-th specialist doctor in the first round). Each
specialist doctor also provides an option ID along with the
corresponding content for the issue at hand. At this stage, each
specialist doctor agent cannot observe the statements made by other
agents.

1: Initialize: Speech pool $`S_{1}=\{s_{1,1},s_{1,2},\dots,s_{1,n}\}`$

2: Round 1:

3: for each specialist $`k`$ do

4:   $`S_{1,k}\leftarrow f(C,Q)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Each specialist
provides an initial response

5: end for

6: $`S_{1}^{4}\leftarrow\text{LeadPhysician}(S_{1})`$ $`\triangleright`$
Process into four viewpoints

7: Store $`S_{1}^{4}`$ in $`H`$

8: Round 2:

9: for each specialist $`k`$ do

10:   $`S_{2,k}\leftarrow f(S_{1}^{4},C,Q)`$

11: end for

12: $`S_{2}^{4}\leftarrow\text{LeadPhysician}(S_{2})`$

13: Store $`S_{2}^{4}`$ in $`H`$

14: Subsequent Rounds:

15: Set $`i=2`$

16: while not $`\text{Consensus}(S_{n})`$ and $`i\leq\text{MaxRounds}`$
do

17:   for each specialist $`k`$ do

18:    $`S_{i+1,k}\leftarrow g(S_{i}^{4},S_{i-1}^{4},C,Q)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Use processed viewpoints from last two rounds

19:   end for

20:   $`S_{i+1}^{4}\leftarrow\text{LeadPhysician}(S_{i+1})`$

21:   Store $`S_{i+1}^{4}`$ in $`H`$

22:   Increment $`i`$

23:   Consensus Check:

24:   if $`\forall k,m\in\{1,\dots,n\}:S_{i,k}=S_{i,m}`$ then

25:    Set $`\text{Consensus}(S_{i})=\text{True}`$

26:   end if

27: end while

28: if not $`\text{Consensus}(S_{i})`$ then

29:   Decision by Majority Rule:

30:   if tie in votes then

31:    Randomly select one answer from agents’ choices

32:   end if

33: end if

Algorithm 1 Multi-Round Medical Consultation

All specialists’ statements are sent to the lead physician(as detailed
in Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Case Studies of the Lead Physician Agent’s Role and Function ‣ Appendix B Additional Details ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")),
who processes them into four distinct components: Consistency, Conflict,
Independence, and Integration.

- •
  Consistency: Aggregates the parts of individual statements that are
  consistent across multiple agent statements.
- •
  Conflict: Identifies and lists conflicting points between different
  statements when the answers are not uniform; otherwise, this component
  remains empty.
- •
  Independence: Extracts the unique viewpoints of each agent, i.e.,
  aspects mentioned by a specific agent but not by others; Remains empty
  if no unique views exist.
- •
  Integration: Synthesizes all agent statements into a cohesive,
  well-structured summary incorporating all perspectives.

The processed statements are denoted as $`S_{1}^{4}`$ and are
subsequently stored in the Historical Shared Pool ($`H`$). Once
statements are stored, the consultation moves to the next round.

Starting from the second round, each specialist doctor agent can access
the structured statements from the previous round, stored in the $`H`$.
They integrate these insights to enhance their prompts and formulate
their responses, denoted as $`S_{2,k}`$, while selecting an option ID
and corresponding answer content for the given issue. As in the first
round, all agents’ statements are sent to the lead physician, who
processes them into $`S_{2}^{4}`$.

From round $`i+1`$ (where $`i\geq 2`$), specialist doctor agents can
review the structured statements from rounds $`i`$ and $`i-1`$, denoted
as $`S_{i}^{4}`$ and $`S_{i-1}^{4}`$, respectively. By integrating
insights from the previous two rounds, they refine their prompts,
articulate their viewpoints, and provide an option ID and corresponding
content for further discussion. The discussion continues until all
specialist doctor agents reach a consensus on the final answer. If a
consensus is not achieved and the number of discussion rounds has not
reached the predefined upper limit (set at 10 rounds), the discussion
proceeds to the next round. If the maximum number of rounds is reached
without achieving consensus, the final decision is made based on the
majority rule. If votes are evenly distributed, the final answer is
randomly selected from the agents’ choices.

Figure 3: Diagram of the residual discussion structure in the MDT
medical consultation process.

This consensus aggregation, combined with the residual discussion
structure (see Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Multi-Round Consultations ‣ 3 Method ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")),
reduces information pollution, enhances discussion efficiency, and
minimizes the cognitive load on the model. The structure limits
specialist doctor agents’ access to deeper memory layers, helping to
prevent excessive influence from other agents and thereby mitigating
hallucinations to some extent. The consultation process follows
Algorithm 1.

### 3.3 Summary and Output Stage

At this stage, the final output ($`C`$) is reviewed by the Safety and
Ethics Reviewer agent. This agent refines and verifies the consultation
outcome, identifies any potential safety concerns, and ultimately
determines the final conclusion ($`R`$). The conclusion is later
validated against the correct result.

If the consultation outcome is accurate, the Chain-of-Thought Reviewer
summarizes and organizes the patient’s background information($`B`$),
medical problem($`Q`$), and the structured statements from the final
consultation round $`S_{\text{final}}^{4}`$. This processed information
is then archived into the Correct Answer Knowledge Base (CorrectKB). The
storage format is as follows:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Conversely, if the consultation outcome is incorrect, the
Chain-of-Thought Reviewer generates an abstract summary of the session.
This summary includes $`B`$ and $`Q`$ and is structured according to the
initial hypothesis, analysis process, final conclusion, and reflection
on error causes. The summary is then stored in the Chain-of-Thought
Knowledge Base (ChainKB). The storage format is as follows:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

When a new patient arrives, their $`B`$ and $`Q`$ are used to retrieve
the $`top-K`$ most similar cases from both knowledge bases based on
cosine similarity computation ($`K`$ = 5 in our application). This
retrieval process enhances the prompts ($`P`$) for the specialist doctor
agents.

To maintain the independent reasoning of each specialist doctor agent,
these two knowledge bases are not referenced during the initial
discussion round. Instead, they are utilized starting from the second
round, particularly in cases where conflicting opinions arise. However,
if a consensus is reached in the first round, these knowledge bases may
be referenced as a reflective measure after the discussion concludes.
The full process is detailed in Algorithm 2.

1: Input: $`C`$, $`B`$, $`Q`$, CorrectKB, ChainKB

2: Outcome Validation:

3: if $`\text{Valid}(R)`$ then

4:
  $`\text{Record}\leftarrow\text{CoT\_Reviewer}(\{C,B,Q,S_{\text{final}}^{4}\})`$

5:   $`\text{Store}(\text{Record},\text{{CorrectKB}})`$

6: else

7:
  $`\text{Record}\leftarrow\text{CoT\_Reviewer}(\{C,B,Q,S_{i}^{4},...,S_{\text{final}}^{4}\})`$

8:   $`\text{Store}(\text{Record},\text{{ChainKB}})`$

9: end if

10: Prompt Enhancement:

11:
$`similarity\leftarrow\text{CosineSim}(B,\text{{CorrectKB}},\text{{ChainKB}})`$

12: $`TopK\_similarity\leftarrow\text{SelectTopK}(similarity,K)`$

13:
$`P\leftarrow\text{Retrieve}(TopK\_similarity,\text{{CorrectKB}},\text{{ChainKB}})`$

14: $`enhancedPrompt\leftarrow\text{Enhance}(P)`$

15: Application of Enhanced Prompt:

16: $`\text{round}\leftarrow 1`$

17: while not $`\text{Consensus}(C)`$ do

18:   $`\text{UsePrompt}(enhancedPrompt,\text{round})`$

19:   $`\text{round}\leftarrow\text{round}+1`$

20:   if $`\text{round}=2`$ and conflicts arise then

21:    $`\text{ConsultKBs}(P)`$

22:   end if

23: end while

24: if $`\text{round}=1`$ and $`\text{Consensus}(C)`$ then

25:   $`\text{ConsultKBs}(P)`$

26: end if

Algorithm 2 Summary and Evolution

It is worth noting that the core model responsible for embedding textual
content into the vector spaces of CorrectKB and ChainKB is OpenAI’s
‘text-embedding-3-small’¹¹ 1
[https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings/embedding-models](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings/embedding-models).

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Datasets

We utilize the MedQA [Jin et al. (2021)](#bib.bib10) and PubMedQA [Jin
et al. (2019)](#bib.bib11) datasets to validate our framework. The MedQA
dataset consists of USMLE-style questions, each offering four or five
possible answers, designed to assess medical knowledge and practical
skills. PubMedQA, based on research paper abstracts, presents questions
with Yes/No/Maybe answers, aiming to evaluate the performance of natural
language processing models in academic question answering. The final
results are based on the test sets of each dataset, with the CorrectKB
and ChainKB containing only experiences from the training sets.

### 4.2 Main Results

In this experimental section, we primarily investigate the zero-shot
accuracy and F1-score advantages of our proposed MDTeamGPT framework in
the context of medical consultations (additional metrics were assessed
through human evaluation, as detailed in
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Human Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Additional Details ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")).
Under this framework, 600 consultation rounds were conducted, during
which the experiences were stored in CorrectKB and ChainKB (MedQA and
PubMedQA each utilized their respective training sets for these
consultations). This benchmark was chosen after considering both
performance and cost. The overall results are shown in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation"),
where gpt-4-turbo serves as the base model across all configurations.

Single-Agent denotes the baseline performance using only gpt-4-turbo;
Single-Agent (w/) CoT incorporates a "Let’s think step by step" approach
in the answering process; Single-Agent (w/) ReAct employs a ReAct-style
prompt, simplified and modified in our experiments to consist of the
"Thought", "Action (Selection)", and "Observation (Reflection)"
processes. Although our approach achieves slightly lower accuracy on the
MedQA dataset than Medprompt [Nori et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23)—likely
because Medprompt is evaluated solely on four-option scenarios—it
outperforms Medprompt on the PubMedQA dataset and in overall averages.
Overall, MDTeamGPT demonstrates strong average accuracy, proving its
effectiveness for advanced LLM-based medical applications.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies

To examine the contribution of each component within the MDTeamGPT
framework, we conducted experiments combining different configuration
settings. Throughout these experiments, gpt-4-turbo served as the
backbone model for all agents.

In Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation"),
the first experimental setting permits all agents to engage in a joint
discussion without any specific discussion strategy; the system only
terminates when either a consensus is reached among all agents or the
maximum number of discussion rounds is exhausted. The second experiment
introduces the residual discussion mode, resulting in lower accuracy on
MedQA but a 0.8% improvement on PubMedQA, leading to a 0.4% decrease in
average accuracy compared with the first experiment. In the third
experiment, we remove the residual discussion mode and only employ the
lead physician to synthesize discussion results. Relative to the first
experiment, this yields a 0.3% drop on MedQA but a 1.4% increase on
PubMedQA, translating into a 0.5% rise in average accuracy.

Notably, combining the residual discussion mode and the lead physician
in the fourth experiment raises the accuracy on MedQA and PubMedQA by
5.8% and 3.6%, respectively, compared with the first experiment,
demonstrating that jointly applying residual discussion mode and lead
physician offers substantial enhancements in consultation efficiency and
accuracy.

We further investigate the role of the two knowledge bases (CorrectKB
and ChainKB) in Experiments 5, 6, and 7, where both knowledge bases
store experiences from 600 consultation rounds. Using only CorrectKB
yields 2.1% and 5.4% higher accuracy on MedQA and PubMedQA,
respectively, compared to using only ChainKB, and leads to a 3.8%
increase in overall accuracy. This finding aligns with intuition, as
CorrectKB Retain verified correct consultation experiences that can
better guide subsequent diagnoses. However, the combined use of both
CorrectKB and ChainKB achieves an accuracy superior to either CorrectKB
or ChainKB alone, corroborating our hypothesis that integrating correct
experiences with reflective insights maximally boosts consultation
accuracy.

### 4.4 Self-Evolving

![Refer to caption](2503.13856v1/fig3.png)

Figure 4: Demonstration of the self-evolving capability of our proposed
MDTeamGPT framework. As the number of consultation rounds increases, the
framework progressively refines its diagnostic accuracy. (A) presents
the performance of our MDTeamGPT tested on MedQA, and (B) illustrates
corresponding results on PubMedQA.

![Refer to caption](2503.13856v1/fig4.png)

Figure 5: Accuracy enhancements achieved by MDTeamGPT over single-agent
baselines across multiple LLMs. (A) depicts the performance boost on
MedQA, and (B) shows analogous gains on PubMedQA. These findings
highlight the framework’s adaptability across language models and robust
efficacy in medical consultation scenarios.

In this section, we evaluate several LLMs — gpt-4-turbo, gpt-3.5-turbo,
gpt-4o, LLaMA3-8B, LLaMA3-70B [Dubey et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7),
glm-4-plus [Zeng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib38), and deepseek-v3 [Liu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib16)—as the core models for our MDTeamGPT framework,
testing their self-evolving capability. Figure
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Self-Evolving ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")
(A) and (B) show how the test accuracy on MedQA and PubMedQA changes
with the increase in consultation samples and stored case experiences.
Regardless of the LLMs used, accuracy improves with more consultation
samples and stabilizes after approximately 600 cases. Figure
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Self-Evolving ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")
shows an interesting observation: LLMs with relatively weaker
foundational abilities, such as LLaMA3-8B, improve faster (steeper
slope) with accumulated consultation experience compared to stronger
models like gpt-4-turbo and gpt-4o.

### 4.5 Framework Efficacy

To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed MDTeamGPT across various
LLMs, we conducted rigorous experiments to assess its performance. The
knowledge bases used in this experiment stored 600 rounds of medical
consultation experiences. Figure
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.4 Self-Evolving ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation")
(A) and (B) compare the accuracy improvements of MDTeamGPT versus
single-agent baselines for each model. The results indicate that all
models benefit from its use, demonstrating both the broad applicability
and enhanced effectiveness of the framework. Although the extent of
improvement varies with the model’s static knowledge and
instruction-following capabilities, our MDTeamGPT framework
significantly enhances medical consultation across different LLMs.

### 4.6 Generalization of the Knowledge Base

We conducted cross-dataset experiments to evaluate the knowledge base’s
generalization and the framework’s overall effectiveness. Using
CorrectKB and ChainKB (constructed from 600 consultation rounds) with
gpt-4-turbo as the backbone, we stored outcomes from one dataset (e.g.,
MedQA) in the knowledge bases and then tested them on another dataset
(e.g., PubMedQA).

[TABLE]

Table 3: Cross-dataset generalization result.

As shown in Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.6 Generalization of the Knowledge Base ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation"),
when using the CorrectKB and ChainKB derived from PubMedQA for testing
on MedQA, the accuracy increased by 3.6% compared to the condition
without any knowledge base; conversely, when using the CorrectKB and
ChainKB derived from MedQA for testing on PubMedQA, the accuracy
increased by 2.1% relative to the baseline without any knowledge base.
These experimental results indicate that the framework not only
successfully transfers specific consultation cases but, more
importantly, effectively migrates the reflective reasoning and thought
processes—abstract cognitive strategies derived from inference and
accumulated experience—to new cases. By preserving reasoning patterns,
CorrectKB and ChainKB not only store consultation examples but also
encapsulate transferable reasoning capabilities, allowing our framework
to generalize across various scenarios.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a novel MDT multi-agent medical consultation
framework, MDTeamGPT, which leverages a residual discussion mode and
consensus aggregation to minimize information redundancy and improve
discussion efficiency. By leveraging two knowledge bases, the framework
dynamically improves overall consultation accuracy and, to some extent,
demonstrates excellent generalization ability. Although the overall
performance of the framework largely depends on the capabilities of the
foundational model used to store and utilize consultation
experiences—which may constrain its performance—our approach still
excels in current medical consultation scenarios.

## Ethical Considerations

This study utilizes publicly available academic datasets and accesses
LLMs via official APIs, ensuring ethical and responsible research
practices. Specifically, the ethical considerations that were taken into
account are outlined as follows:

Public Datasets: The medical datasets used in this research are publicly
released and intended for academic purposes. No personal patient data
was involved or processed.

Licensed API Usage: Our use of LLMs adheres to the API usage policies,
maintaining compliance with fair use standards and respecting
intellectual property rights.

Transparency: We provide detailed descriptions of our experimental
methods to ensure the reproducibility of our results, and we are
committed to promoting transparency in scientific practices.

## Limitations

Our study provides a comprehensive set of experiments to assess the
performance of the proposed MDTeamGPT. However, several areas could be
further improved and explored in future research.

Increasing Agent Complexity: Currently, the agents in our framework are
defined quite simply. We believe that by incorporating more advanced
techniques, such as Tree-of-Thought [Yao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib36), or
integrating external tools and knowledge bases, we could significantly
enhance the reasoning capabilities of the multi-agent medical
consultation system.

Expanding the Dataset: In our experiments, we have used only two
datasets—MedQA and PubMedQA. To strengthen the validity of our findings,
future work will involve testing on a broader range of datasets, which
will help confirm the robustness of our method across different types of
data.

Testing in Real-World Scenarios: Our research has mainly focused on
experiments with pre-existing datasets. In future work, we aim to
collect more real-world consultation data, which will allow us to assess
how well our framework performs in practical, real-life settings and
explore its ability to generalize beyond controlled experimental
environments.

Figure

### B.3 Human Evaluation

[TABLE]

Table 4: MDTeamGPT Human Evaluation Questionnaire.

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of MDTeamGPT, we invited
five volunteers to participate in the tests. All volunteers hold at
least a bachelor’s degree in clinical medicine, and two of them have
medical practitioner qualifications. We randomly selected five questions
from the MedQA dataset and five questions from the PubMedQA dataset,
resulting in a total of 10 test questions. Volunteers observed the
outputs of MDTeamGPT and rated them using the survey questionnaire shown
in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.3 Human Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Additional Details ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation").
Each volunteer was assigned integer scores for every test. The
evaluation covered 10 dimensions: accuracy, explainability,
completeness, rationality, diversity, efficiency, consistency, user
experience, safety, and innovation. This portion of the testing was
conducted using gpt4-turbo.

As shown in
Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ B.3 Human Evaluation ‣ Appendix B Additional Details ‣ MDTeamGPT: A Self-Evolving LLM-based Multi-Agent Framework for Multi-Disciplinary Team Medical Consultation"),
the volunteers assigned relatively low scores to the "Efficiency"
metric, primarily due to the increased time required for multi-round
discussions among multiple roles compared to the Single-Agent approach.
The "Diversity" metric also received an average score below 3. This may
be attributed to the Temperature setting of 0.7, which was chosen to
balance determinism and randomness; increasing this value could
potentially enhance diversity. For "Completeness", the average score was
3, though some feedback indicated that certain responses lacked
sufficient consideration. To address this, future improvements will
focus on designing more comprehensive prompts and optimizing the
framework’s efficiency. All other metrics received scores above 3,
demonstrating the potential value of MDTeamGPT in practical medical
applications.
````
